about: The PSS feature model: the axes an app developer chooses, their values, the constraints between them, the bricks each value needs, and the blueprints (the few robust combinations). docs/design-guide/README.md is the decision guide over it, and python3 -I scripts/check-design-space.py --plan <blueprint> prints one blueprint as a starting plan.

Conditions ('if', 'require', 'when'): an object maps axis ids to the list of value ids it accepts; every listed axis must match (AND), values in one list are alternatives (OR). {'any': [c1, c2]} is OR of conditions, {'not': c} negates. A missing condition means always. The pseudo-axis 'example' names an entry of 'examples'.

constraints: when 'if' matches and 'require' does not, the constraint applies. level 'error' marks a combination the design forbids (REGISTER, the parser or the contract library refuses it, or it defeats the axis's purpose); 'warn' marks a sensible but costly or not yet built choice. 'msg' is the reason. 'fix' is the nearest valid choice.

bricks: one module per responsibility. 'kind' is 'interface' (the seam of an axis or a shared service) or 'implementation' (one supported value behind an interface, named in 'implements'). 'path' is where the brick lives, or will live when its status is 'to-build'. 'api' is the structured list of the library items an app calls, by where it calls them ('contract': the Noir contract libraries; 'circuit': pss_core; 'client': pss-client and the e2e driver; 'machine': what an operator configures), each {symbol, path}, with an optional 'note'; a brick an app never calls says 'internal' with the reason. check-design-space.py checks that every symbol is defined in its file, that the examples use no library item outside the api lists ('apiCheck'), and renders docs/design-guide/BRICKS.md from the bricks and the axes.

A value's 'bricks' lists brick ids, or {'id', 'when'} entries that apply only under a condition. 'coreBricks' are used by every permutation. A blueprint's 'bricks' must include the core bricks and every brick its values need; it may add others.

leakage: the leakage table of the design guide, one row per intake: who sees the inputs, the requester, what is on chain, who sees the state and the outcome, whether funds are at risk when all three nodes' secrets leak (invariant 0), and what the nodes' knowledge is worth to an adversary ('worth').

parties: the guide's one table of what each party sees under the recommended design (secret-shared receipt intake, node-held state, partial-note completion), what it adds under a deviation, what it can do to funds, and what its knowledge is worth.

compatibility: the lego claim made explicit. Any value of one axis combines with any value of another unless a rule forbids the pair. Each rule names the constraints it covers (every constraint belongs to exactly one rule), its scope ('permutation': one app's choice of values; 'namespace': the rounds of one deployment, which one permutation cannot show), where it is enforced and the section that states it ('link'). The pairs no valid permutation contains are derived from the error constraints: python3 -I scripts/check-design-space.py --compat prints them, and the design guide carries them in generated blocks.
Edit this file, then run: python3 -I scripts/check-design-space.py --write-readme && python3 -I scripts/check-design-space.py --write-bricks && python3 -I scripts/check-design-space.py.

built.label: built
built.desc: In the tree and tested (unit, TXE, three-party or e2e).

to-build.label: to build
to-build.desc: Designed (ARCHITECTURE.md or DECISIONS.md); not built yet.

option.label: kept option
option.desc: Built, not the default, and kept as an option beside it.

deferred.label: deferred
deferred.desc: A supported later option; REGISTER refuses it until it is built.

not-offered.label: not offered
not-offered.desc: Named so the design can say why it is refused: no design and no code; a constraint forbids it.

experimental.label: experimental
experimental.desc: An option offered for trial, never a default and never in a blueprint, with its leakage and cost stated beside the recommended value.

external.label: external
external.desc: A third party's code the design depends on: a published dependency, never vendored or built here.

axes.label: Path
axes.question: Does the result land in the requester's own private function, or through a public queue at the tip of the chain?
axes.help: Follows from the intake: 'direct' is the sidecar path, every queued intake is the tip. Not a manifest field of its own.

values.label: sidecar path (private function)
values.note: The user's own private function verifies the co-SNARK, nullifies the state notes it consumed and creates the new ones. No queue: the client sends POST /v1/execute itself.
pros: one transaction, the user's own, composable with any other private call
no relayer, no queue, no chain reader
cons: a round commits at the nodes before its transaction lands: shared state under contention serialises through the users' transactions, and a node row whose transaction never lands stays ahead of the chain until the operator rolls it back

values.label: tip of chain (public queue)
values.note: Requests join a FIFO queue in the app contract; the orchestrator's scheduler runs the head against the current state; a result transaction verifies the proof privately and applies it publicly.
pros: many users transition one shared state without racing for a note
ordering is the chain's, not the users'
cons: an operator-run scheduler, chain reader and relayer
a result lands one queue turn later, never inside the user's own transaction
deployment takes a secret salt, REGISTER before deployment and a once-only configure

axes.label: State mode
axes.question: Where does a key's state live between rounds?
axes.help: Manifest field state {keyref: client | node | chain}, per key. In every mode the state is Rep3 shares to the nodes and a hiding commitment to the world.

values.label: client-held records
values.note: The user carries a sealed state record (one third per node, sealed by the nodes to themselves) and presents it at the next round. Sidecar path only.
pros: the nodes keep no state rows
state that belongs to one user stays with that user
cons: the user must keep the record (FETCH recovers it from the orchestrator)
a requester key signs every request that presents a record

values.label: node-held
values.note: Each node keeps its Rep3 pairs; the chain holds one commitment per key (a tree root for a tree-valued key). On the sidecar path a node row; at the tip versions anchored to the queue.
pros: nothing but a commitment on chain
the state grows with the store, not with a log
cons: recovery depends on the nodes' stores (backups and resync from two neighbours)

values.label: chain-held (sealed in every apply)
values.note: Every apply logs the whole new state sealed to the nodes' keys. Recovery needs those keys, the package that decodes the log, and a matching log from the previous 64 queue entries or the init round. For small, fixed-size states only, isolated in one module per layer behind the state interface.
pros: recovery from a matching log without the nodes' state stores
cons: the whole state is broadcast on every apply, bounded by the transaction's public-log capacity (a few hundred elements)
the sealed state stays on chain for good: anyone who later learns two nodes' enc scalars, or breaks the Grumpkin key exchange, opens every past state

axes.label: State shape
axes.question: Is one key's state a small fixed vector, or a large or growing collection?
axes.help: A flat key is one vector loaded whole. A tree-valued key is a Poseidon2 Merkle tree of depth D with leaves of w fields; a round touches at most K leaves (the probe width), so its cost depends on K and D, never on the number of leaves in use. Manifest field tree {keyref: {depth, leaf_len, probe, ...}}. The clear-index tree (the nodes know which leaves a round touches) is the recommended tree; the oblivious tree, which hides the index from the nodes, is an experimental option.

values.label: flat vector
values.note: One vector per key (the AMM's reserves are 3 elements, Monty Hall's game 10).
pros: simplest circuit and store
one commitment over the whole state
cons: every round loads and rewrites the whole vector, so the circuit grows with the state

values.label: Merkle tree, clear index
values.note: The recommended tree. Touched leaf indices are clear to the nodes (no oblivious access); leaf and internal hashes are public data each node keeps in the clear; every written leaf takes a fresh blinding. Good enough for most books because the index names no one: under partial-note completion the owner's address never enters the circuit, so a node that sees index 41 touched learns that position 41 moved, not whose it is.
pros: capacity of 2^D - 1 leaves at a circuit width set by K
one root commits to the whole book (a header leaf holds pool-level fields)
cons: K·D shared Poseidon2 permutations per round, sequential in depth, so link latency sets witness-extension time
a node sees which leaves each request touches and can link requests on one position
under a secret-shared intake nobody, the owner included, sees a position in the clear except through its own rounds

values.label: Merkle tree, oblivious index
values.note: Experimental: the tree's leaves and internal hashes live in a distributed oblivious RAM (GigaDORAM, vendored from gigadoram-rs on the pinned co-snarks), and the index is a shared input bound through C, so no node learns which leaves a round touches (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, 'The oblivious tree'). The manifest's tree entry says access: oblivious; the dense brick (indexed positions) is built as machine/sidecar-oblivious with its recovery (resync, share refresh, backups) built and its audit specified; the sparse keyed map with non-membership proofs is the shape value map_oblivious. Not a default: the clear-index tree is recommended. The escape hatch works on it as on the clear tree: an exit tag needs no index and no path.
pros: the nodes do not see which positions a request touches, so they cannot link a position's requests or tell which positions are active
a liquidation's probes and a scan's window are hidden from the nodes too
cons: experimental: the DORAM is a new joint state with no production history whose audit is specified, not built, and whose cost on a real link is projected from in-process numbers (about 200 sequential communication steps per lending round, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, 'The DORAM and its measurements')
the old paths become shared Poseidon2 permutations too (2·K·D sequential in depth) and every slot is written back, so witness extension and the round's MPC time grow
it hides the index from the nodes only; the world never saw it, and a full compromise still opens every leaf

values.label: Keyed map, oblivious (sparse Merkle tree)
values.note: Experimental: a sparse Merkle tree of depth 32 to 120 over a key's low bits, held in the same distributed oblivious RAM as the oblivious tree, addressed by (height, prefix) with a capacity-bounded lazy bottom level (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, 'The oblivious sparse map'). The manifest's tree entry says access: oblivious, keyed: true; each index input is a key (an owner commitment, a hashed name), the leaf's first element is the key, and an empty leaf on a verified path proves the key absent. For state addressed by a key rather than a position: credits paid to a key before its owner acts (examples/credits-tip), registries, spent-identifier sets. No header, no openings, no windows: nobody can enumerate it, so a book a third party must scan (lending's keeper) stays on a tree.
pros: membership and non-membership proofs on the committed root along the key's own bits; insert, update, lookup and prove-absent as one read and one write
no node learns a key, a path, whether a key was present or whether a round inserted
memory follows the addresses ever accessed (each new key about 2(depth - log2 keys) + leaf_len + 3), never 2^depth
cons: experimental, on the oblivious tree's unbuilt audit and unmeasured link cost, plus a widened DORAM address (128-bit) measured in-process only
2 * K * depth shared Poseidon2 permutations per round (256 at depth 64 for two keys) and depth + 1 + leaf_len DORAM accesses per slot (68), about four times lending's

a bounded capacity counted in accesses: about 285 keys keep working at the default capacity 2^18 (reads of absent keys cost addresses too); past it every round is refused (409, the keyed map is full), and a map has no grow path, so a deployment sets its capacity with headroom
the fill count is opened at each bottom-level rebuild (the order of the key count)

no escape hatch: a keyed map has no tagged write (when the shares do not open C its private write re-blinds the slots at the keys the prover chose, so it cannot keep the exit tag's rule that such a round writes no entry)
collision resistance rests on the app supplying hashed or random keys

axes.label: Intake
axes.question: How do a request's inputs reach the network, and who may see them?
axes.help: Manifest field intake. 'direct' is the sidecar path; every other intake queues the request at the tip. The default here is the recommendation (the examples' default); a manifest that names no intake takes direct. One compiled circuit per round serves each intake family (<round> both non-secret-shared intakes, <round>_shared both secret-shared intakes): the round takes its inputs as private witnesses bound through the commitment C = poseidon2(inputs, blinding), and the intakes of a family differ only in who computes C. One source per round, compiled once per family it runs under.

values.label: direct execute
values.note: The client POSTs /v1/execute to the orchestrator. PUBLIC inputs are clear to the nodes; INPUT_SHARED inputs reach each node as one Rep3 pair in an envelope.
pros: no queue, no receipt, no intake transaction
cons: sidecar path only

values.label: on-chain intake
values.note: The user's private function appends the request; the inputs and a random user_nonce go into a public request log, and no address does. A test path: inputs and outputs public.
pros: no off-chain step before the request transaction
anyone can audit every input
cons: the world sees every input; a state the initial value and the inputs determine is public
the round type shows through the clear inputs

values.label: receipt intake
values.note: The client sends the inputs to the nodes over TLS and gets three Schnorr receipts, which the user's private function checks before it appends the request. A test path.
pros: no input reaches the chain
the world sees only the request id and the expiry block
cons: the three nodes and the orchestrator see every input and can follow the state in the clear
outputs stay public

values.label: secret-shared receipt intake
values.note: The examples' default. The client sends each node one Rep3 pair of every sensitive input and a hiding commitment C; the nodes check C inside the MPC; nothing but the request id and the expiry reaches the chain.
pros: no party but the user holds an input, and nobody holds a touched state value in the clear
no ciphertext of an input ever reaches the chain (post-quantum for the inputs)
the round type can be hidden
cons: an off-chain step (the receipt) before the request transaction
the outcome must be private (private outcomes)

values.label: secret-shared on-chain intake
values.note: The user's private function derives the shares itself and puts them in one private log, encoded so only the nodes can open them, and stores its hash beside the queue entry; node enc keys live in public storage and rotate by a node transaction. Shares secret-shared receipt intake's round circuits, MPC receipt check and result path. The clear app inputs sit in the clear in that log. Built in the machine, the contract library, pss-client and the AMM tip and lending examples: the AMM tip's swap and lending's deposit register their secret-shared round's circuit again under it (TXE, three-party and e2e cases).
pros: no off-chain step: the request transaction is the whole intake
the same privacy as secret-shared receipt intake
cons: the encoded shares stay on chain for good: anyone who later learns two nodes' enc scalars, or breaks the Grumpkin key exchange, opens every request's inputs
the clear app inputs are public in the request log (a lending position's index links the requests on it), where secret-shared receipt intake shows them to the nodes and the orchestrator only

values.label: relayed intake
values.note: The network submits the request transaction for the user. No design; REGISTER refuses it.
pros: the user sends no transaction
cons: not composable when the user's own transaction culminates in the request
no design

axes.label: Binding
axes.question: Which state does a queued request run against?
axes.help: Manifest field binding (queued intakes only). No interface of its own: the manifest and the circuit carry it.

values.label: none (sidecar path)
values.note: A sidecar-path request names the record or node row it loads; the contract checks that note exists.

values.label: turn
values.note: Apply to the state as it is when the request's turn comes. A total circuit turns a request the state no longer allows into an ok = 0 no-op.
pros: a request never goes stale because another landed first
cons: the user cannot pin the state it saw (slippage limits belong in the inputs, e.g. min_out)

values.label: exact
values.note: Bind to the state the request saw: the circuit folds old_c == bound_c into ok. REGISTER refuses it.
pros: the result is exactly what the user simulated
cons: under contention most requests land as no-ops

axes.label: Outputs
axes.question: Who may learn the round's outcome?
axes.help: Public outputs are proof public inputs (and, at the tip, whatever apply stores). Private outcomes are outcome notes plus one private log, which only the user can open; apply then only marks the request resolved and writes the commitments. Follows from the intake family: private under a secret-shared intake, public under every other intake. Not a manifest field of its own.

values.label: public outputs
values.note: Sidecar path: proof public inputs, seen by the user, the orchestrator and the nodes. Tip: apply's app hook stores them where the world sees them. The non-secret-shared intakes keep public outputs, since their inputs are public anyway.
pros: no outcome encryption, no outcome discovery
cons: at the tip the world learns the outcome and, from it, often the state

values.label: private outcomes
values.note: The result transaction's private function pushes the outcome note hashes the circuit computed and emits the outcome ciphertext in a private log padded to 16 fields; the user finds it by its tag and opens it with its outcome key.
pros: the outcome reaches the user only
the slot write reveals nothing about ok (a fresh blinding on every outcome)
cons: outcome encryption and a note-hash computation inside the MPC
the client must discover and deliver the outcome note

axes.label: Value delivery
axes.question: Does the round move value to the user, and in which transaction?
axes.help: Manifest field outcome (queued intakes only): partial (the default) | none. 'partial' is partial-note completion: the user commits a partial note (owner and randomness) in its request and the network completes it, inside the co-SNARK under private outcomes or in apply under public outputs; the completed note is a standard note of the app contract that the result transaction lands, nothing value-bearing shown to the nodes, the orchestrator or the relayer, no second transaction; ownership across rounds is proven in the user's private function by opening the completed note (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, 'Partial-note delivery'). 'none' completes no note: the round's public outputs go to the app's hook in apply. REGISTER refuses none under a secret-shared intake, whose outcome reaches the user only by partial; a non-secret-shared manifest that completes no note says outcome: none (an init round); the sidecar path takes no outcome field and is always none. So it follows from the intake: partial under a secret-shared intake, none on the sidecar path, and under a non-secret-shared intake each round's own field (partial when it completes a note, none when it completes none), never an app-wide choice.

values.label: no value moves
values.note: No library delivery: the round completes no note. At the tip, under a non-secret-shared intake only, the public outputs go to the app's hook in apply (a counter, an outcome map by queue index; machine/circuits/tip_counter), and an init round, which delivers nothing, says outcome: none. On the sidecar path the user's own transaction lands the result, so any value moves in the app's own code there (a game's reveal, a swap's effects).
pros: nothing to complete or redeem
cons: at the tip a public output that one user should own is readable by everyone and owned by nobody, and the app keeps its own store and reader for it

values.label: partial-note completion
values.note: The request commits a partial note (its owner and randomness) and the network completes it with the round's outcome, so the value lands with the result as the user's own note. Built in the libraries, the machine, the AMM tip (completion in the co-SNARK for the secret-shared swap, in apply for the non-secret-shared swap) and lending (completion in the co-SNARK for every secret-shared round, in apply for the non-secret-shared deposit; ownership by note); the recommendation and the default under every queued intake. The user's private function commits P = poseidon2_sep([owner, rho], DOM_SEP__PARTIAL_NOTE_COMMITMENT) (aztec-nr's partial-note convention) as the reserved shared value $partial_note; the round completes the note inside the co-SNARK (private outcomes: the completed note hash poseidon2_sep([storage_slot, P, outcome fields, request_id], DOM_SEP__NOTE_HASH) is a public output, the fields reach the user in the outcome ciphertext) or apply completes it in public (public outputs: the standard completion log, the user hidden behind P). Ownership of a position is proven in the user's private function by opening its completed note and committing the next partial note to the same owner, never inside the MPC. One randomness rule for every example: rho, $outcome_key and $outcome_tag derived by the client from its wallet secret and a request counter. A refund the user may be owed (an escrow, a deposit) is a second partial note that a public function completes, never a round (skip() only with the stale period enabled and a skip wrapper that calls token::refund_skipped). See docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, 'The refund rule'. The requester, and a handle's holder: a request commits one partial note, of an owner the sender's PXE holds (partial_note::commit), and the round completes that one; a party other than the requester (a liquidated owner, an auction's winner, an employee) receives value or information from another party's round only through a standing delivery handle its own request left in its entry (the delivery-handle brick), else through a round of its own on a note of its own.
pros: value lands with the result: no second transaction
nobody but the user sees the amount or the owner: the nodes, the orchestrator and the relayer see ciphertext and hashes
ownership is proven in the user's private function, never in the MPC (invariant 0): a full node compromise moves nobody's value
the owner's view of its position is its own note (minimal PSS)
cons: a position note is never nullified, so an owner's view can be stale after another party's round that finds no handle of the owner's (a second liquidation before the owner's next request) until its next round or a view
the request function reads a note for an owner-bound round (the standard cost of a note read)
a public result's completion log shows the amount to the world (the owner stays hidden)

axes.label: Delivery
axes.question: Must the circuit guarantee that data for someone other than the nodes is correctly created and encrypted?
axes.help: Verifiable delivery. Constrained: the circuit computes the ciphertext (Poseidon2 duplex AEAD under a key the recipient supplied, such as the one-time outcome key, so no key exchange inside the MPC) and exposes it with the note hashes as public outputs, so a result lands only if the recipient can open it. Rule: constrain anything value-bearing or needed to spend (note preimages, outcome plaintexts); public data is a public output of the proof and needs no encryption. Data sealed to a node itself (client-held and chain-held record thirds) is sealed by the nodes outside the circuit: a node that seals garbage can only halt, which any single node can already do. Node-sealed delivery to a user is not offered. Withholding data entirely is a liveness question no constraint fixes. Follows from the outputs, and so from the intake family: constrained for private outcomes, clear for public outputs.

values.label: nothing private to deliver
values.note: The outcome is a public output; the proof constrains it and every party that sees the outputs reads it.
pros: no encryption
cons: public

values.label: constrained in the circuit
values.note: The outcome ciphertext and note hashes are public outputs of the round; nonce poseidon2([note_hash, SIDECAR_OUTCOME_AD]) over the completed note's hash, which commits to the plaintext, so one nonce seals one plaintext.
pros: a misbehaving node cannot land a result the user cannot open or spend
cons: the AEAD and the note hash cost shared Poseidon2 permutations in every round

values.label: sealed by the nodes
values.note: Not offered to users: the nodes would encrypt the data to the user after the round, outside the circuit. Node-sealed delivery exists only for record thirds sealed to the nodes themselves, which is not this axis's value.
pros: no encryption gates in the circuit
cons: a node can deliver garbage that still lands; the recipient sees the failure but no proof binds it

axes.label: Submission
axes.question: Who sends the transaction that lands the result?
axes.help: One lander (fetch, prepare, send, retry) with a policy. At the tip process_result is open to anyone.

values.label: user (or anyone)
values.note: Sidecar path: the user's own transaction. Tip: pss-client submitResult sends the same process_result a relayer would.
pros: no operator dependency for landing
cons: at the tip the user must watch the queue and pay the result transaction

values.label: pss-relayer
values.note: Operator-run, tip only: FETCHes the head's result, sends process_result, sends skip() when the head is stale, lands the init round; pays every transaction through the private fee-payment contract.
pros: users send only their request
cons: an operator service to run and fund

axes.label: Node keys
axes.question: May the network's node keys change after deployment?
axes.help: The key set every node signature is checked under: the three nodes' sig keys (and the enc keys on record), epoch 0 being the constructor's pins. Chosen in the contract, at compile time: the last type parameter of the app's round table rows (KeyEpochs or FixedKeys), which the library's signature checks take their keys from, and under key epochs the four entry points the app declares. The contract manifest states it as node_keys (generated: rotating exactly when the artifact has rotate_keys), which replace-node and the scheduler read; on chain a contract with a fixed key set never writes the key-epoch slot and reads as key epoch 0 for good. Tip only: on the sidecar path no contract checks a node signature (the user's own private function verifies the proof), so neither value adds a brick there.

values.label: key epochs (rotating)
values.note: The contract keeps a numbered key set, a key epoch, at the library's own storage slot; two of the three current nodes sign the next set, and the contract accepts the previous set's signatures for stale_blocks blocks after the rotation lands. How a lost, departed or compromised node is replaced without redeploying the app (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md section 6, 'Node replacement and key epochs').
pros: a lost, departed or compromised node is replaced in place: the same address and state, the queue paused during the replacement
one stolen key cannot rotate the set (two signatures), and a departed node cannot veto its own removal (two, not three)
a rotation is public and dated: the honest third, every client and every relayer see one they did not approve the moment it lands
cons: more public bytecode: the credits example measured 18,208 bytes under key epochs against 13,250 with a fixed key set (4,958 bytes, 27%), about 5,450 of the lending example's 36,923 bytes (15%)
every private function that checks node signatures (results, the init, receipts) reads the key-epoch slot at its anchor and enqueues a public epoch check
the replaced node's signatures still verify for stale_blocks blocks after the rotation lands
two colluding current nodes can rotate the set (two nodes already learn every shared value, and no key authorises a move: invariant 0)

values.label: fixed key set
values.note: The constructor's sig keys for the life of the contract (FixedKeys in the round table rows; examples/credits-tip): no key-epoch slot, no rotation entry points, the signature check under the pinned keys alone, as constrained as under key epochs. A lost or compromised node cannot be replaced without redeploying the app (a new salt, a new address and an empty state). A node's enc key for secret-shared on-chain intake still rotates by the node's own signed transaction (check_enc_rotation::<FixedKeys> verifies it under the node's pinned sig key). The machine and the clients read the never-written key-epoch slot as epoch 0, the constructor's keys; after a node replacement the orchestrator computes nothing for the namespace, and replace-node's rotate_keys line for it cannot land.
pros: smaller public bytecode: none of key rotation's code (the credits example 13,250 bytes against 18,208 under key epochs; the lending example about 5,450 bytes less than its 36,923 under key epochs)
no key-epoch read and no enqueued epoch check in a result's, the init's or a receipt's private function
who signs for the contract never changes, so a client checks against the pinned keys alone
cons: a lost or departed node halts every round for good, and a compromised sig key stays one of the three: either way the fix is a new deployment under a new salt (a new address and an empty state), which every user moves to (a tree's owners exit through the escape hatch)
nothing on chain tells it from a contract that has not rotated; its contract manifest's node_keys does, so a node replacement prints no rotate_keys line for it but names it for redeployment

axes.label: Upgrades
axes.question: May the app's circuits, or its contract's code, change after deployment?
axes.help: What about a deployed app may change. Chosen in the contract, at compile time: where its private functions take their circuit pins from (CircuitsInForce: FixedCircuits, the stored Configured as it is, or CircuitUpgrades, pins an upgrade authority the constructor pins may replace after a delay) and, when upgradable, the upgrade_circuits entry point the app declares. The contract manifest states it as upgrades (generated: contract when the artifact has upgrade_contract, circuits when it has upgrade_circuits, else fixed) and, when not fixed, storage.circuit_pins, where every node and the scheduler read the pins in force. Only a namespace that is not fixed takes a replacement contract manifest, and each round runs under the version the pins name. Under circuits and contract the package list holds at most 14 and 13 packages (one upgrade rewrites 4P + 6 public slots, a class upgrade 4 more, and a transaction writes at most 63), and queue.stale_blocks must not be null: a request queued under a replaced circuit is never answered, and only skip() frees the queue of it. Tip only: on the sidecar path no contract pins a circuit, so neither value adds a brick there.

values.label: fixed circuits
values.note: The constructor's circuit pins (the contract manifest's hash, the package list, the vk hashes) for the life of the contract, in the stored Configured (FixedCircuits; examples/credits-tip, examples/lending-tip). No upgrade function, no delayed value and no upgrade authority; a new circuit is a new deployment. Only as fixed as the class: the library adds no call to the protocol's ContractInstanceRegistry.update.
pros: the smallest bytecode and private functions: nothing read beyond Configured and no upgrade function
nothing new to trust: nobody can change the rules of the shared state after deployment
cons: a circuit bug is fixed only by a new deployment under a new salt (a new address and an empty state), which every user moves to

values.label: upgradable circuits

constraints.msg: The sidecar path has no queue and no intake transaction: the client sends POST /v1/execute itself.
At the tip every request enters through the queue: pick a queued intake (secret-shared receipt intake is the default).
Binding is a queue notion: a sidecar-path request names the record or node row it loads.
A queued request binds to its turn or to an exact state.
Chain-held state is sealed into the apply log of a queued result; the sidecar path has no apply log.
A client-held record is presented by its owner in its own request; a queued request has no requester to present it, and REGISTER refuses client-held keys under a queued intake.
Tree-valued keys are node-held tip keys: the nodes keep the clear tree of hashes and the leaves as versions anchored to the queue.
Under access: oblivious every index input is INPUT_SHARED, since a clear index would show the nodes the leaf, and the non-secret-shared intakes take no INPUT_SHARED input.
On the sidecar path the result lands in the user's own transaction; pss-relayer serves the queue only.

Under a secret-shared intake nobody holds a touched state value in the clear; public outputs would publish what the shares hide. The outcome is private and apply only marks the request resolved and writes the commitments.
The outcome key and tag travel as shared inputs, so private outcomes need a secret-shared intake. The non-secret-shared intakes keep public outputs: their inputs are public anyway.
Under a secret-shared intake the outcome is private and reaches the user only as the completed note of its own partial note; REGISTER refuses outcome: none there.
On the sidecar path the user's own transaction lands the result, so the app's own code moves any value there; REGISTER refuses an outcome field under intake direct.
A public output is read in the clear by everyone who sees the outputs; there is nothing to encrypt.
A private outcome must be encrypted to the user.
Value-bearing data, or data needed to spend (the outcome note's preimage), is encrypted inside the circuit, so a misbehaving node cannot land a result the user cannot spend.
Node-sealed delivery to a user is not offered: it has no design, and a node could hand the user garbage that still lands. Data for a user is constrained in the circuit or public.

The oblivious tree and the keyed map are experimental: REGISTER accepts access: oblivious (and keyed: true) under the secret-shared intakes, the bricks run in the machine with their resync, share refresh and backups built and their audit specified, not built. The oblivious tree keeps the escape hatch; a keyed map has none (there is no tagged map write). The clear-index tree is recommended: the nodes see which positions a round touches, but under partial-note completion no position names its owner.
Relayed intake is deferred with no design; REGISTER refuses it.
binding: exact is deferred and REGISTER refuses it. Its design: the request carries the slot values it saw and the circuit folds old_c == bound_c into ok.
Secret-shared on-chain intake keeps the encoded shares on chain for good (harvest now, decrypt later). Secret-shared receipt intake keeps every input ciphertext off chain.

Chain-held state broadcasts the whole state, sealed to the nodes, on every apply: for small, fixed-size states whose operators need recovery without the nodes' state stores. The sealed states stay on chain for good.

Secret-shared receipt intake keeps inputs off chain, but chain-held state puts every new state on chain sealed under the Grumpkin key exchange, so a later key compromise opens the state history anyway. Secret-shared on-chain intake is the consistent pairing.

The non-secret-shared intakes are test paths: the inputs are clear (to the world under on-chain intake, to the nodes and the orchestrator under receipt intake), outputs are public and the round type shows. A key takes rounds of one intake family only, so non-secret-shared rounds run on a deployment of their own.

A node row on the sidecar path advances at the nodes when a round commits, before its transaction lands: a later round loads the new row, and its transaction fails at the contract until the earlier one lands; a transaction that never lands leaves the row ahead of the chain until the operator rolls it back (DESIGN.md, operator procedures). For shared state under contention use the tip.
With a fixed key set a lost, departed or compromised node cannot be replaced: the app is redeployed under a new salt (a new address and an empty state) instead.

Upgradable circuits trust an upgrade authority, which can change the rules of the shared state and take the value it controls after the delay: tell the app's users who it is. The contract manifest's stale_blocks must not be null.

compatibility.about: Any value of one axis combines with any value of another unless a rule below forbids the pair. The decision axes are the ones a developer picks; path, binding, outputs, value and delivery follow from them. The intake family sets outputs, value and delivery, three combinations in all: a secret-shared intake gives private outcomes, partial-note completion and constrained delivery; a non-secret-shared intake gives public outputs, clear delivery and, per round, partial or none; the sidecar path's direct intake gives public outputs, no value delivery and clear.

bricks.name: Escape hatch

api.note: the app keeps its liveness period (lending's Config::t_live), its exit function (lending's exit(position, request_id): read the sender's note, Hatch::exit, then pay what the note says) and its outcome note's ExitNote impl; an app without per-owner entries can use Hatch alone (the clock, the opening and the refusals) with an exit rule of its own

bricks.does: Exit from a frozen app with no node (the liveness half of invariant 0): each owner of an entry leaves privately on its newest note, with one nullifier and no public call. The circuit half (pss_core tip::exit): a round that writes an entry of a tree-valued key stores in the new leaf the exit tag of the note it issues for that entry, exit_tag(P, request_id, entry) = poseidon2([PSS_EXIT_TAG + 2^128·entry, P, request_id]) with P that note's partial commitment, and outputs the tag it replaces, or a filler, the same number of values on every round type; a note names an entry only if its round wrote it; a round whose shares do not open C writes no entry. The contract half (pss_public_contract hatch, one storage slot): every request wrapper and poke() start the starving clock (Hatch::queued); every landing refuses once open, emits the round's exit tags as nullifiers in the public call that moves the commitment and stops or restarts the clock when the round served its request (Hatch::landed; skip() and a round whose shares did not open C leave it); open_hatch() opens it for good once the clock reaches the app's liveness period (Hatch::open; lending's Config::t_live, default 20,000 blocks); then no request is queued and no round lands, skip() and redeem keep working, and the private exit (Hatch::exit) checks that the sender's note names an entry and that the hatch was open at the anchor block, and pushes the note's exit tag, which succeeds once and only on the entry's newest note. The app pays what the note says (lending: a borrower repays y and receives x, a lender receives y; no interest since the note's round). An app needs a secret-shared intake with partial-note outcomes, per-owner entries in a tree whose leaf spares one element, an outcome field that names the entry, every round that writes an entry issuing its owner a note (its own, or a delivery to a handle it left) and a rule for what a note pays; a keyed map has no tagged write. Lending uses it on every deployment, the oblivious one included; the plain deployment's notes hold nothing to exit. The chain sees one nullifier per landing and per exit, never an entry. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md section 6, 'The escape hatch'; examples/lending-tip/README.md, 'The escape hatch'.

api.note: lending's assert_holds is app code over these

bricks.does: Ownership proven in the user's private function by opening its completed note (partial-note chaining), never inside the MPC: the round has no owner check, the leaf no owner element, and a full node compromise acts on nobody's position (invariant 0). A note with code = 0 and a nonzero position is an owner note of that position; notes are never nullified, so a skipped request costs no ownership, an index is never reassigned, and a position note's payout is spent through a redeem nullifier of its own while the note stays; the owner's view refreshes with its next round, a view, or a liquidation's notice to its delivery handle.

bricks.name: Standing delivery handle
bricks.does: Delivery to a party other than the requester: a round another party requested completes the recipient's standing handle, the partial note completed with the round's fields for the recipient and the note's packed fields encrypted to the handle's key, so the recipient learns of it privately with no round of its own. A handle authorises nothing (its partial commitment binds the recipient: invariant 0) and is not used up: every round that writes the entry may complete it until the recipient's next request writes a new one, and each completion is another note, logged under its own tag poseidon2([key, PSS_HANDLE_TAG, request_id]). Every round of an app that uses it outputs the same deliveries (a filler seeded from the request's blinding where nothing is delivered), so the round type and whether anyone was notified stay hidden; an app without it pays nothing. Lending is the worked example: every request on a borrower position refreshes its handle, and a liquidation completes the liquidated owner's with the position after the liquidation and keeps it (about 780 gates on the liquidation, about 540 to 630 on every other round). docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, 'The standing delivery handle'.

One trait, SigningKeys, with one implementation per value (key-epochs, fixed-keys); every library entry point that takes a round table row verifies the three node signatures under the keys its implementation returns, so the brick chooses which keys, never whether the signatures are checked (invariant 0).

bricks.name: Key epochs

api.note: an app names KeyEpochs<E> in its Keys alias, which its round table rows take (TipRound<C, R, W, Keys>), E the enc keys the contract holds (KeyEpochs<SharedOnchain<PublicContext>> under secret-shared on-chain intake, else KeyEpochs<NoEncKeys>), and declares four one-line entry points over the contract items (rotate_keys, set_node_keys, assert_key_epoch, get_node_keys); set_node_keys hands Keys::install that E (its SharedOnchain, or NoEncKeys {}), so the install voids a replaced node's enc key, and secret-shared on-chain intake takes only a brick that does (RetiresEncKeys), so the two cannot disagree; the library's result, init and receipt checks call key_epoch::signing_keys through it

bricks.does: The numbered key set (a key epoch: the three nodes' sig and enc keys) every node signature is checked under, and its rotation by two of the three current nodes; KeyEpochs, the SigningKeys implementation an app names in its round table rows. Epoch 0 is the constructor's sig keys; rotate_keys checks two current signatures over the next set and installs it at the library's own storage slot; signing_keys, inside every result, init and receipt check, verifies under the current set or, for stale_blocks blocks after a rotation, the previous one, and enqueues the app's assert_key_epoch. The contract manifest states node_keys rotating; the machine signs the next set in sidecar-node replace-node (sidecar-core key_epoch) for every namespace whose manifest says so, and the scheduler computes nothing while a contract's set is not the configured one; pss-client reads the contract's epoch (keyEpochNode) to check signatures and seal envelopes to the current keys. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md section 6, 'Node replacement and key epochs'.

api.note: an app names FixedKeys in its round table rows (TipRound<C, R, W, FixedKeys>) and check_enc_rotation::<FixedKeys> if it takes secret-shared on-chain intake, and declares none of rotate_keys, set_node_keys, assert_key_epoch or get_node_keys; the library's result, init and receipt checks take the constructor's keys through it

bricks.does: The node signature check under the constructor's sig keys for the life of the contract: FixedKeys, the other SigningKeys implementation (pss_public_contract signing_keys). No key-epoch slot, no rotation, no anchor read and no enqueued epoch check; none of key_epoch's code reaches the app's bytecode. The contract manifest states node_keys fixed (generated: no rotate_keys in the artifact); the never-written key-epoch slot reads as epoch 0 everywhere, so the nodes, the scheduler's key-set gate and pss-client work under the pinned keys unchanged; after a node replacement the gate computes nothing for the namespace (its message names the fixed key set and redeployment), and replace-node prints no rotate_keys line for it but names it for redeployment. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md section 6, 'A fixed key set'.

bricks.does: The upgrades seam: where a private function takes the circuit pins it verifies under. One trait, CircuitsInForce, whose in_force returns the stored Configured with the pins in force, with one implementation per value (fixed-circuits, circuit-upgrades); the round table built from its result pins the vk hashes in force.

bricks.name: Fixed circuits

api.note: an app on fixed circuits takes its round table rows from FixedCircuits {}.in_force over the stored Configured (the identity) in the one function every round function calls, and declares no upgrade function; its contract manifest says upgrades fixed and has no storage.circuit_pins

bricks.does: The circuit pins under the constructor's values for the life of the contract: FixedCircuits, the CircuitsInForce implementation that returns the stored Configured as it is. No delayed value, no authority, no upgrade function and none of the upgrade code in the app's bytecode. The contract manifest states upgrades fixed (generated: no upgrade_circuits or upgrade_contract in the artifact); REGISTER refuses any other contract manifest for the namespace (the same one re-enables its packages). docs/ARCHITECTURE.md section 7, 'Upgrades'.

bricks.name: Circuit upgrades

api.note: an app declares CircuitUpgrades<P, DELAY, Context> last in its storage, pins the authority in its constructor (init), builds every round function's rows from CircuitUpgrades::in_force over its stored Configured and declares two wrappers: the public upgrade_circuits and the #[only_self] assert_upgrade_class over CircuitUpgrades::assert_class, which CircuitUpgrades::in_force enqueues from every round function (examples/amm-tip); the owner registers the new contract manifest at the next seq and the authority schedules its pins (upgradeCircuits over circuitPinsOf); a client follows the version in force (readCircuitPins, adoptManifest)

bricks.does: Circuit pins an upgrade authority may replace after a delay: CircuitUpgrades, a DelayedPublicMutable of UpgradedPins (the class id, the contract manifest's hash, the package list and the vk hashes) and the authority the constructor pins, and its CircuitsInForce implementation, which returns the stored Configured under the scheduled pins once in force (the constructor's while none was ever scheduled); the read caps the transaction's expiration below the next time of change. upgrade_circuits checks msg_sender against the authority and no node signature (invariant 0), checks the list as the constructor does and schedules the pins under the current class. REGISTER accepts a replacement contract manifest under check_upgrade's rules (the contract's facts and each state key's layout unchanged, no new key, the same intake family), keeps up to three versions, and reuses the vk of a circuit whose bytes a held package stores; each node's chain verifier, the scheduler and the receipt route run a round only under the version whose hash the pins name at their block (ChainReader::manifest_in_force). docs/ARCHITECTURE.md section 7, 'Upgrades'.

bricks.name: Class upgrade

api.note: an app on upgrades contract declares the circuit-upgrades brick and one more public wrapper, upgrade_contract over CircuitUpgrades::upgrade_contract (examples/amm-tip); the developer publishes the new class, the owner registers its contract manifest at the next seq, the authority calls upgradeContract, and every wallet and the relayer register the instance again with the new artifact (followContractClass; the relayer's upgradeArtifacts); pss-manifest verify checks a deployed contract against a contract manifest

bricks.does: The move of an instance to another contract class with the circuit pins of the contract manifest built for it: CircuitUpgrades::upgrade_contract checks msg_sender against the authority, calls the protocol's ContractInstanceRegistry.update (the class must be registered), refuses unless the instance's class-update delay equals the pins' delay, and schedules the pins under the new class, so both take effect at one timestamp. The pins carry their class, the constructor records the original one (UpgradeAuthority), and every round function enqueues assert_upgrade_class, which refuses pins of another class than the one running: old code never runs with new pins, nor new code with old ones. REGISTER takes the new class's contract manifest under check_upgrade's class rules (the state keys, the circuit pins' slot, the package capacity, upgrades and a rotating key set kept; slots only the code reads may move); each reader runs a round only while the instance's current class is the class of the version the pins name. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md section 7, 'Upgrades'.

blueprints.label: Sidecar path, client-held state
blueprints.suits: State that belongs to one user and is hidden from everyone, the user's own future moves included: games against the house, per-user sealed commitments, private counters and allowances, credentials whose use the network enforces.
pros: one transaction, the user's own, composable with any private call
no queue, scheduler or relayer
the nodes store nothing between rounds
cons: the user keeps its records (FETCH recovers a lost one)
one evaluation per state: the consume-once policy, not the circuit, stops a second evaluation, so each round's single reveal must be safe

deviations.use: shared state with little contention, where the result must land inside the user's own transaction
deviations.cost: a round commits at the nodes before its transaction lands, so concurrent users wait on each other's transactions and a transaction that never lands needs the operator's rollback; the nodes keep a row per key

blueprints.label: Tip, node-held state, secret-shared receipt intake
blueprints.suits: A small, fixed-size shared state that many users transition and nobody may see, where every round pays nobody but its requester: AMM pools, a private counter or rate limiter shared by an app's users, a treasury whose rules bind the requesters, a sealed-bid auction's best bid when the auction settles to nobody but each round's requester (one that pays its winner keeps a leaf per bid: tip-tree).
pros: nobody holds an input or a touched state value in the clear, the nodes included
no input ciphertext reaches the chain
the round type is hidden by default
value lands with the result as the user's own completed note; nobody but the user sees the amount or the owner (partial-note completion)
cons: an operator-run scheduler and relayer

on the receipt route the orchestrator sees the user's network address beside C, so it can link that address to the request on chain and the result's outcome tag (a relay or a mixnet to the orchestrator hides it, outside the build)
state recovery depends on the nodes' stores

questions.ask: What must be shared at all?

answers.answer: Nothing: every value belongs to one user and needs no hidden rule enforced by others. Use plain Aztec notes and private functions; no PSS.
One user's state must stay hidden from that user too (a game against the house, a sealed commitment): the sidecar path with client-held state.

Some state must be computed on by many users and seen by none (a pool's reserves, a book's positions, a sealed auction's bids), or drawn on under rules the network enforces while its owner is offline (a treasury its members claim from): put only that essential part on PSS and keep ownership, balances, outcomes, escrow and refunds as user-owned notes. A round pays or informs its requester only, so every party that must receive value or information acts in a round of its own on an entry and a note of its own.

questions.ask: Who must not see the state and the inputs?

answers.answer: Nobody but the user may hold an input or a state value in the clear, the nodes included (two colluding nodes still could: state what that is worth, such as front-running a trade within its min_out or the first liquidation of every unhealthy position).
The world must not; the three nodes may see inputs (test or trusted-operator deployments).
Only the requester's identity is private; inputs may be public.

questions.ask: Is the state per user or shared by many users?

answers.answer: Per user: one owner transitions it.
Shared, with little contention, and the result must land inside the user's own transaction.
Shared by many users who act concurrently.

questions.ask: Is the shared state small and fixed, or large and growing?

answers.answer: Small and fixed (a few dozen fields).
Large or growing, and each round touches a few entries.

questions.ask: May the nodes see which entries of a tree a round touches?

answers.answer: Yes (recommended): the index names no one under partial-note completion; the nodes learn that a position moved, not whose it is.
No: the oblivious tree (positions) or the keyed map (keys, with non-membership proofs), both experimental.

questions.ask: Must the state be recoverable without the nodes' state stores?

answers.answer: No: node backups and resync from two neighbours are enough.
Yes, the state is small and fixed, and the operators have the keys, the package and a matching log from the previous 64 queue entries or the init round.

questions.ask: May the user's request need an off-chain step (a receipt from the nodes) before its transaction?

answers.answer: Yes: keep every input ciphertext off chain.
No: the request transaction must be the whole intake.

questions.ask: Who may learn the round's outcome?

answers.answer: The requester only: private outcomes (implied by a secret-shared intake).
Everyone: public outputs (the non-secret-shared intakes and the sidecar path's proof outputs).

questions.ask: Does the round move value to the user?

answers.answer: No value moves: the outcome is information only, or the sidecar path's own transaction moves it (outcome: none, refused under a secret-shared intake).

Yes: the user commits a partial note in its request and the network completes it, so the value lands with the result as the user's own note and nobody but the user sees the amount or the owner (the default). Apps that take escrow or a usage deposit commit separate refund notes that public functions complete. With the stale period enabled and a skip wrapper that calls token::refund_skipped, a skipped request gets those refunds without a round.

questions.ask: Is the data the user receives value-bearing or needed to spend?

answers.answer: Yes (an outcome note, a payout): constrain it in the circuit.
It is public anyway.
An operator-run relayer.
The user (or anyone).

questions.ask: May the network's node keys change after deployment?

answers.answer: Yes (the default): a lost, departed or compromised node is replaced in place, by a key epoch two of the three current nodes sign.
No: the constructor's keys for the life of the contract, for smaller public bytecode; replacing a node then means redeploying the app.

questions.ask: May the app's circuits change after deployment?

answers.answer: No (the default): the constructor's circuits for the life of the contract; a fix is a new deployment.
Yes, the circuits: an upgrade authority the app names may replace the circuits after a delay, in public; the contract's code stays.
Yes, the circuits and the contract's code: the authority may also move the instance to another contract class after the same delay; users trust it as they trust an upgradable contract's upgrader.

properties.label: Invariant 0: a leak of all three nodes' secrets puts privacy at risk and can freeze funds, never take or lose them
properties.text: An adversary holding every node's enc and sig scalar, every share and every store, and running the orchestrator and the relayer, can open every value and run and sign any registered circuit on any inputs; it must still move nobody's value and lose none. Consequences: no value a circuit trusts as an authorisation is a shared input or a node-held value (ownership is proven in the user's private function over a user-owned note); the circuits a contract pins are committed by its address, never by node signatures; escrow, deposits and refunds are user-owned notes that public functions complete; a frozen market has an escape hatch that needs no node (lending's), which bounds a freeze only against nodes that stop: nodes that keep landing rounds while refusing service keep it shut. Met by the contract library: nodes that deviate and flag a round's shares as not opening C (code 14) set its public inputs-opened bit, and apply refunds that round's escrow; what remains is liveness, not a take: an owner round refused on its leaf's own state (lending's codes 4 and 5) re-blinds the leaf and names no entry, so the owner's earlier note does not exit until its next round. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md section 5 checks every brick against it.

properties.label: Minimal PSS: only the essential shared state is PSS
properties.text: Everything that need not be shared stays user-owned private state (Aztec notes): ownership, a user's balances and positions, outcomes, escrow and refunds. Only what must be shared is PSS: a book's aggregates, a pool's reserves, what another user's round must probe or scan (lending's liquidator and keeper). The first question of a design is what can leave the PSS; value delivery is partial-note completion (in the co-SNARK for a private result, in a public function for a public one), to the requester only: a round completes the one partial note its request committed, of an owner the sender's PXE holds, so every party that must receive value or information acts in a round of its own on a note of its own (lending: the liquidator is paid its seize, the liquidated owner refreshes with a view). Built in every tip example (examples/lending-tip/README.md, 'What is a note, what is shared', gives lending's split).

properties.label: The requester is hidden from the chain and the nodes
properties.text: On every intake: no msg_sender in an intake function, no user in a request id, request log, receipt or receipts row ($user refused at REGISTER); ownership, where an app needs it, is proven in the user's private function over a user-owned note (built: lending's note ownership). Built for on-chain intake, receipt intake and secret-shared receipt intake, with a requester audit in the contract, machine and client suites and in the AMM tip's and lending's three-party cases and e2e scenarios, and for secret-shared on-chain intake, whose request the library's and the examples' TXE suites and the examples' secret-shared on-chain e2e scenarios audit; under secret-shared on-chain intake the user never meets the orchestrator. Not hidden from the orchestrator on the receipt routes (receipt intake and secret-shared receipt intake): it sees the user's network address beside the inputs or C, hence the chain request id, and so can link that address to the request on chain, the result's public outcome tag and the timing of a later redeem. A user who must hide it reaches the orchestrator through a relay or a mixnet (a deployment's deviation, outside the build).

properties.label: Fees through a private fee-payment contract
properties.text: Every tip transaction (request, result, redeem, configure, init, enc rotation, skip) pays through Wonderland's private fee-payment contract, so the fee payer is that contract for everyone; paying from the user's own account names the user and undoes the hidden requester.

properties.label: Trust model
properties.text: Rep3 over three operator-run nodes, honest majority: one node alone learns nothing and can only halt; two colluding nodes learn every shared value. Node count and threshold are fixed.

properties.label: Node replacement
properties.text: A signed node-key epoch, a numbered key set (sig and enc together): the constructor pins key set 0; two of the three current sig keys declare the next set (rotate_keys); every signature-checking function verifies under the current set or, for G = stale_blocks blocks after a rotation, the previous one, and the epoch is the one its signatures verify under; the two remaining nodes refresh every sharing (a fresh zero-sharing added to every stored pair, nothing reconstructed) before the newcomer imports its pairs from them; the handshake's summand hashes, the npk_app_hash check and the audit round check it; the orchestrator pauses scheduling for refresh, import, audit and declare, and takes the key set from its configuration (ARCHITECTURE.md section 6, 'Node replacement and key epochs').

properties.label: Verifiable delivery
properties.text: Data for anyone other than the nodes, if value-bearing or needed to spend, is encrypted inside the circuit under a recipient-supplied key and exposed as public outputs (the delivery axis). Record thirds for the nodes are node-sealed. Withholding is a liveness question. Built in the libraries (outcome encryption, the completed note and the outcome log) and in every tip example's secret-shared rounds; the AMM tip's and lending's completed notes are each opened by their owner in the three-party cases and the e2e scenarios.

properties.label: Total, co-noir-compatible round circuits
properties.text: A queued round must be total (no input makes it unsatisfiable; a bad request is an ok = 0 no-op with a code). No ECDSA inside the co-SNARK, no integer bit operations in Brillig (total-noir's entries other than those its page "co-noir compatibility of the library's hints" excludes); scripts/check-noir.sh gates both.

properties.label: Hidden round type
properties.text: Under a secret-shared intake: one request wrapper and one apply per app with uniform arguments, pinned reads and effect counts, logs padded to 16 fields; a round type stays visible only where it must change genuinely public state. Built in every tip example; the AMM tip's and lending's TXE suites check it (test_round_shape.nr: the public calls, the effect counts, every private log's length and the metered gas of every round type's request and result, under one gas setting per kind). Timing stays visible.

properties.label: Ordering
properties.text: One FIFO queue and one lock per namespace; the scheduler pipelines on the latest attempt of a live entry. Sharding across queues is not designed.

properties.label: One intake family per namespace
properties.text: A non-secret-shared-intake package may not read a key in a namespace where a secret-shared-intake package writes one (the init round, which reads no key, sits beside the secret-shared rounds); non-secret-shared test rounds run on a deployment of their own. REGISTER applies it to the namespace (sidecar-core registry/register_rules.rs, intake_families_clash), since a manifest names its keys only by position: the key-reading non-secret-shared packages and the key-writing secret-shared packages of one namespace never mix. Per key is the future enhancement, for a multi-book namespace that wants mixed families.

properties.label: Deployment
properties.text: A secret random salt, the packages compiled and their vk hashes computed locally, the contract manifest generated from the artifact and REGISTERed in one manifest message before deployment, a constructor that pins the circuits (the node sig keys, stale_blocks, the package list, each package's vk hash, app constants: the address commits to the circuits, invariant 0), a once-only configure of the signed npk_app_hash; new circuits are a new deployment. The permissionless, signature-checked configure is one workable approach; an app may entrust its deployer instead.

properties.label: One compiled circuit per round per intake family
properties.text: Every round of every tip example but its init round runs under the default intake (secret-shared receipt intake); the non-secret-shared intakes (on-chain intake and receipt intake) run on one round of the AMM tip and of lending (the swap, the deposit) as the test path; one compiled circuit per round serves each intake family, its inputs bound through the commitment C, with Noir generics or comptime only where a public-input layout must differ. Artifacts may multiply; code does not. Built for the non-secret-shared intakes: one layout, the inputs private and the request id a proof output, one compiled circuit and one process_result per round. Built for the secret-shared receipt rounds of every tip example: each round's source under one secret-shared main (the private outcome in place of the non-secret-shared outputs), such as amm_swap_tip_shared and lending's ten *_shared circuits; secret-shared on-chain intake takes the same secret-shared circuits: the AMM tip's amm_swap_tip_shared and lending's deposit_shared are registered again under it, as each non-secret-shared circuit is under both non-secret-shared intakes.

parameters.label: stale_blocks
parameters.where: the contract manifest (queue.stale_blocks); the contract checks its configured value against it
parameters.text: How long a head may wait before skip(); null disables skip. skip() returns what the skipped request put in (its usage deposit and any escrow) into its refund notes. Under secret-shared receipt intake each node's REGISTER refuses null and a period whose receipt life outlasts its enc grace window. Under upgrades circuits or contract REGISTER refuses null: a request queued under a replaced circuit is never answered, and only skip() frees the queue of it.

parameters.label: depth D, leaf_len, probe width K
parameters.default: per app, measured: K the largest width at which every round fits 2^14 gates
parameters.text: REGISTER bounds a round by K and D.

parameters.label: consume policy
parameters.text: never only for a key a round reads without spending.

parameters.label: init strategy
parameters.text: A seed round (sidecar path), an in-round SAMPLE, or public constants; at the tip the scheduler sends the init round once configured.

parameters.label: access control
parameters.where: the app's request and skip() wrappers
parameters.text: Permissioned requests are the app's own check in its private request function; the machine admits every request. The pattern is a credential note of the app's own type (minted to the holder at deployment or by a round), read with its inclusion check and never nullified, as lending's assert_holds reads a position note; never a shared input, which the nodes could forge (invariant 0). A round so gated is already priced by its note, so the usage deposit is for the open rounds. Who may call skip() is the app's skip() wrapper's check, anyone by default.

parameters.label: outcome fields
parameters.text: One outcome shape for every round of an app, so a ciphertext does not tell the round type.

parameters.label: pinned-read freshness
parameters.where: manifest public_reads[].freshness (epoch_param, band); the pinned-read check of apply, the scheduler and the chain verifier
parameters.text: Per pinned read: exact (apply requires the value used), epoch (the source returns [value, epoch, previous]; the circuit takes the value and its epoch; apply accepts the current epoch or the one before, so a round lands while at most one new epoch opens during it; epochs are u64s; the source offers previous only within a window of blocks after an epoch opens, lending's oracle for previous_blocks) or tolerance (an absolute or relative band). Each node's chain verifier admits a request's own value by the policy on an entry's first attempt only, later attempts at its own read. Under exact a value that moves faster than a round lands starves the head until skip(). The lending tip's price read uses epoch, its clock read (the market's own block number, to which its rounds accrue interest) tolerance with an absolute band of 128 blocks.

parameters.label: usage deposit
parameters.where: the request's private function (pss_public_contract token, the UsageDeposit pin): a pinned amount of a pinned token drawn from the user's private balance in the app (lending: one Credit note, beside the escrow), with a refund note of the app's credit type that binds the amount (token::commit_refunds)
parameters.default: per app; the library refunds it when the round runs (UsageDeposit::kept = false); lending: its borrowed asset, kept by the protocol
parameters.text: The queue's anti-spam. Nothing public names the requester or the amount: the request moves no token, and its public wrapper records the refund notes' commitments only. The token is the app's choice, and so is the settlement: kept by the protocol, or refunded (a DEV DECISION on UsageDeposit::kept). In an app that takes escrow or a usage deposit, a public function completes the refund note with the request id alone (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, 'The refund rule'). When the stale period is enabled and the skip wrapper calls token::refund_skipped, skip() returns any escrow and the deposit without the nodes. For a landed round, apply returns or keeps the deposit as the app chose and refunds it when the shares did not open C (lending's code 14). A deposit kept on skip or on a round that served nobody is forbidden in every app: a network that skips heads must never earn from it, and a liveness failure must not reach funds (invariant 0). A request whose private balance does not cover it reverts in its own transaction: nothing is queued.
